text.en: The Gemara's leniency to use inferior wicks and oils on Chanukah becomes a statement about souls: Chanukah reaches Jews whom even Shabbos cannot set alight.
The halachah that the Chanukah lamp belongs below ten tefachim, the one place the Shechinah never goes, shows that on Chanukah Hashem descends to those who cannot ascend.
The hidden light conceals itself by nature, which is why Yosef's brothers and Yehuda failed to see the light of Mashiach in Yosef and in Tamar until it was revealed.
The name Chashmonaim spells Chodesh, Shabbos, Milah and Ner: Hashem answered the Greeks' attempt to uproot three mitzvos by adding a fourth.
The single sealed flask of oil that the Greeks could not defile is the hidden point of faith in every Jew, which no impurity can reach.

The Rav applies the Mishnah's practice of salting a cow's womb, so that it loves the calf born in pain, to explain why the Rambam calls Chanukah, acquired with mesiras nefesh, an exceedingly dear mitzvah.

The Rav suggests that the name Chashmon is an acronym of Chodesh, Shabbos, Milah and Ner: since the Greeks sought to uproot three mitzvos, Hashem added a fourth, just as the Midrash says He answered Haman with Purim.

Because the Greeks invaded the Beis HaMikdash, a domain that was not theirs, the Rav explains that Chanukah answers measure for measure by invading the domain of tumah: night, the left side, the public domain and the longest nights of Teves.

The Rav reads 'vayehi kehayom' in Yosef's trial as the twenty-fifth day, the tekufah when the nations held their festival and no Torah was learned, and sees Chanukah on the twenty-fifth as its counterweight.

The Rav explains that the letters of Yavan, yud, vav and final nun, are one point stretched ever lower, showing the Greeks spreading in tumah, while Chanukah's lights spread more each night in kedushah.

The Rav contrasts Shabbos, when a Jew rises to the kedushah, with Chanukah, when the kedushah descends below ten tefachim; this is why even inferior oils and wicks are allowed on Chanukah, and why souls that Shabbos does not reach can be kindled.
The empty receptacles of the menorah, which seem to contradict the rule that a brachah rests on fullness, are themselves the message: they are souls still waiting to be kindled.

The reshus harabim, whose very name means 'the many', stands opposite the oneness of the Yachid shel Olam, yet the Chanukah lights were meant to be lit there to bring kedushah into the territory of tumah.
The Satan targets the finer souls, which is why returnees are often more devoted than those born into observance.
Unlike the seven-branched menorah of the Beis HaMikdash, the Chanukah menorah's eight lights show what the menorah will be like when Mashiach comes.
Each night's added light is another soul retrieved from the Satan's captivity, and the eighth night corresponds to Mashiach, when no receptacle will remain empty.
The thirty-six hours of the hidden light correspond to the thirty-six tractates of Shas and to the thirty-six candles lit over the eight days of Chanukah.
Shechem, whom the Rav calls a monster, carried a spark of Mashiach ben Yosef; Hashem hid it there as one hides a diamond in a garbage can, where thieves and the Satan would never look.
The Chanukah candle is the one mitzvah that draws the Shechinah below ten tefachim, into the domain of the Satan, to bring out holiness from there, and this is the pattern of Mashiach.
Dina, who was first conceived as Yosef, provided Yosef's match through Osnas, and the letters of her name spelled out in full equal Mashiach ben Yosef in gematria.
Yaakov hiding Dina in a box was no accident: she belongs concealed, because she is the Chanukah light and the hidden light.
Ovadia, a convert from Esav, prophesies Esav's downfall, like the axe whose handle is cut from the very forest it chops down.
The wicks and oils that burn poorly stand for souls that Shabbos cannot ignite; on Chanukah the Shechinah comes down to them, so they are fit for Chanukah lights.
The Beraisa says 'on the 25th of Kislev the days of Chanukah are eight' without 'begin', because in the Mikdash all eight days were literally one day, the 25th.

The Kohanim's crying was not over a lost mitzvah but over the Menorah above: as long as the Menorah below burns, the Menorah above glows and sends light and blessing; if it goes out there is galus and darkness.
The Kohanim lit naturally, not by a miracle: Hashem, who prepared at creation the nature for now and the nature for later, moved the nature of Yemos HaMashiach into the time of the Chashmonaim.
The Rambam holds back the laws of Hallel until the end of Sefer Zmanim, in the laws of Chanukah, because hallel and thanks are the particular blessing of Chanukah.

Every feature of Chanukah breaks the Jewish preference for favorable times and places: end of the month instead of its first half, left instead of right, night in Teves, the public domain, below ten tefachim. The Rav reads this as Chanukah being the Yom Tov of the deepest galus.

Going out to the public domain is going out of Hashem's 'atmosphere', which is why carrying out on Shabbos is forbidden; lighting there means conquering territory from the Satan and bringing back neshamos that fell to the side of the yetzer hara.

The candle is the neshamah ('ner Hashem nishmas adam'), so the Chanukah lights kindled in the dark stand for blown-out neshamos given a new sparkle, and the words 'haneiros halalu kodesh hem' refer to them.
The Rav reads the Midrash on 'Vayehi ba'eis hahi' as the answer to the questions of our own dark time: each of the Avos and Shevatim was busy with his own trouble, and Hashem was preparing Mashiach.
The dark episodes of the parsha produced both Mashiachs: from Dina and Shechem came Asnas, Yosef's wife and the source of Mashiach ben Yosef, and from Yehudah and Tamar came Mashiach ben David.

A mitzvah is like a button at the bottom of the Empire State Building that turns on every light: our 248 limbs correspond to 248 mitzvos, and each movement brings light or the opposite into the world without our seeing how.
The Rav argues that the Greek rule of accepting only what one understands is itself illogical, since the mind grasps only a tiny part of what exists; it is emunah that is logical.
Emunah is not only belief but faithfulness, the instinctive loyalty of a wife to her husband; the Avnei Nezer shows such an instinct is reliable enough that a woman may remarry on one witness.
Levi felt the bond with Hashem more strongly because Levi's very name came from the bond of husband and wife, which is why Levi answered 'Mi laShem elai' both with Moshe and with Matisyahu.
Klal Yisrael bears the name Yisrael as a wife bears her husband's name: 'yashar' joined with Hashem's Name.
Because tumah is a barrier in the bond with the pure G-d, a war against emunah is in essence a war of tumah; the Greeks entered the Heichal to defile rather than to destroy.

The pach shemen, the symbol of taharah's victory, was hidden under the very marble slab from which the dust for the sotah was taken, the place that testifies to the purity of a wife and of Knesses Yisrael.
Yaakov needed the name Yisrael from the angel before Beis El because he would first face Shechem, which, like Yavan, sought to rip out the name Yisrael.

The Rav reads the halacha that wicks unfit for Shabbos may be used for Chanukah as a statement about souls: Jews too distant for the light of Shabbos to touch can still be kindled by the light of Chanukah.

Chanukah is the one exception to the rule that the Shechinah never descends below ten tefachim; its light is placed below ten tefachim, in the public domain and on the left side, because it goes down into the domain of the Sitra Achra to reach the souls there.
Unlike every other Yom Tov, which falls at a full or growing moon, Chanukah falls at the end of the month in the longest nights, so that every Jew, whatever his level, can find his place in it.

Both Mashiach ben Yosef and Mashiach ben David came through people whose greatness was hidden and misjudged: Yosef seen as a tyrant, Tamar taken for a zonah, Yehuda rejected by his brothers; this concealment is itself the hidden light of Mashiach.
A spark of Mashiach ben Yosef was hidden in Shechem, the way a person hides a diamond in a garbage can so no one will steal it, and Dina had to draw it out to join it with her own spark.
Spelled out with the full names of its letters, the name Dina has the gematria of Mashiach ben Yosef, showing that her purpose was set from her birth.
The Rav calls emunah a created instinct, parallel to the appetite for food: Hashem builds a desire into whatever a person needs, and a person needs emunah to reach the purpose of his creation.
He explains Greek rationalism as a means rather than an honest search: by declaring that only proven things are believed, the Greeks freed themselves from the yoke.

Because an instinct must be gratified, the Greeks who denied G-d did not stop believing; they redirected the instinct of emunah onto physical strength and beauty, which the Rav sees as the root of sport and of fashion worship.
Like Moshiach, whose gematria equals nachash because he repairs what the snake spoiled, Chanukah has the gematria of guf, because it stands against the worship of the body.
The order Ein k'Elokeinu before Mi k'Elokeinu teaches that one may not ask the question about Hashem before first stating the answer.
Matisyahu, the soul of Chanukah, equals 'Beis HaMikdash' in gematria, so in the days of Chanukah a Jew merits a Beis HaMikdash.
The word chashman hints at chodesh, Shabbos and milah, the three mitzvos the Greeks tried to abolish, together with ner Chanukah, the mitzvah Hashem added in response.
On Shabbos a Jew is raised to the higher world, while on Chanukah the higher light descends into the weekday of exile; this is why the Shabbos light may be used and the Chanukah light may not.
The words of the psalm's blessing, 'Hashem will bless you from Zion and you will see the good of Yerushalayim', equal 'ner Shabbos, ner Chanukah' in gematria.
The letters of 'bracha' are each the first doubling in their rank of numbers (two, twenty, two hundred), showing that blessing means increase.

Achitofel's Torah was barren: nothing grew from his two teachings, yet David called him rebbe; all the more so one whose chiddush gives rise to further chiddushim, which is the meaning of 'children of your children'.

Aharon's bashfulness kept him from the nesi'im's bold voluntary offering, and his consolation was precisely that his descendants would one day need holy boldness, to defeat Yavan, the kingdom of brazenness.
The 'ox' on whose horn the Greeks demanded the Jews write was the golden calf: their claim was that a nation capable of serving it has lost its bond with Hashem.
A bas Levi who remarried on a false report loses maaser because she lacked the trait of Levi, the inner sense of an essential bond that would have told her that her husband was alive.
Chanukah has no festive meal because it celebrates the hidden essential bond, which cannot be displayed, unlike the festivals whose greatness was shown in the Beis HaMikdash service.
Chanukah's light is revealed more as history approaches Moshiach: barely mentioned in the Mishnah, it expanded greatly from the Arizal and the Ba'al Shem Tov onward.

Following Rebbe Tzadok HaKohen, the extra verse of redemption added beyond the alphabetical order of a chapter of Tehillim shows a conduct above the natural order, by which Hashem does not let any Jew be lost.

Dovid HaMelech ruled on questions of purity himself because, as king of all Israel with a soul from Atzilus, his ruling to permit a wife to her husband acted in all the worlds on the bond of Israel with Hashem.

Just as oils that will not burn well enough for Shabbos may be lit on Chanukah, there are Jews whom Shabbos cannot kindle but Chanukah can, because on Chanukah the Shechinah comes down to them rather than asking them to rise.
The slave who chose to stay is freed only by yovel, the 'eighth'; so too Chanukah, which is of yovel, can free a Jew whom the 'seven' of Shabbos cannot.
Shabbos is sanctified with wine, of the world of seven, while Chanukah is sanctified with oil; shemen shares its root with shemoneh, eight.
Oil rises above every other liquid, like fire that always rises, because it belongs to the higher world of the eighth and strives back to its source.

Yevamos, Eruvin and Nidah are the hardest masechtos because all three deal with the coming of Moshiach: the tikkun of souls, turning the world into a reshus hayachid, and ending the exile likened to nidah.
The Chanukah light set at the door, in the public domain, brings the light of Moshiach into the reshus harabim and so makes it a reshus hayachid.

Chanukah is the one time the Shechinah breaks its own rule of not descending below ten tefachim, because it comes for Jews who are themselves 'below ten', in the public domain rather than the domain of the One of the world.
Following the Tur Bareket, the Chanukah light precedes the Shabbos light because it is elevated and enters into the Shabbos light, so a low, weekday light rises into Shabbos.

The Chanukah miracle fell at tekufas Teves, the longest night, in a month left to the sitra achra and at the end of the lunar month: the darkest point from every side is exactly where the Shechinah came down.
Ner, pesilah and shemen form the initials of neshamah, so the oils and wicks unfit for Shabbos but fit for Chanukah stand for souls that Shabbos cannot kindle but Chanukah can.
Yosef's test on the idolaters' festival day was so great because on that night one does not learn, so he lacked the Gemara's advice of Torah learning as protection.
Even a wicked informer who lit Chanukah lights shone in all the worlds; had he grasped that light and repented, it would have accompanied him into the morning Hallel and protected him.
Unlike the Hallel of the Yamim Tovim, Chanukah's Hallel is an obligation on weekdays, which is why the Rambam places all the laws of Hallel in Hilchos Chanukah, the end of Sefer Zmanim.

Following the Chasam Sofer, Yaakov's wish to dwell in tranquility was not a desire for ease: having lived out every sign of galus through Gog uMagog, he sought to be the sign of the days of Moshiach, but this world has no vessel for such a sign, so instead galus began anew with Yosef.

Emunah in what is beyond the intellect is real because every Jew has some measure of ruach hakodesh, and that is why the Greeks, who wanted to uproot it, attacked through tumah, which cuts a Jew off from his pure neshamah.
Though impure oil could have been used, the beauty of the miracle was that the oil was pure, symbolizing the victory of 'tamei'im b'yad tehorim'.

The jar of oil was most likely hidden under the loose stone from which the sotah's dust was taken, so it was guarded in the very place that guards the purity of Jewish daughters, which was what the Greeks sought to destroy.
Esav, unable to bite Yaakov, kissed him; the Rav sees this as the tactic of the nations before Moshiach, who seek to destroy Jews through embrace and togetherness rather than persecution.
Chanukah, read as chaf-heh, alludes to the 25 letters of Shema Yisrael, because emunah includes not only that Hashem is One but also that one is Yisrael, the very point the Greeks attacked.

Yaakov's insistence on the angel's concession at once, rather than at Beis El, is explained by the coming encounter with Shechem: the name Yisrael was the weapon against Yavan, which is why the angel fought so hard against conceding it.
Matisyahu, the 'soul' of Chanukah, is in gematria 'Beis Hamikdash': in the days of Matisyahu every Jew merits a Beis Hamikdash in his own home.
Lighting the menorah needs no kohen while preparing it does, because the lighting already belongs to the light of the future, when every Jew will be a kohen.

The letters of Chashmon hint at chodesh, Shabbos, milah and ner: the three mitzvos the Greeks tried to abolish and the mitzvah of ner Chanukah that was added in response, as Purim was added when Haman resented the Jewish festivals.

One may enjoy the Shabbos light but not the Chanukah light, though both are the hidden light, because on Shabbos a Jew is raised to a higher world, whereas on Chanukah that world comes down into weekday exile, where it is not yet the time to use it.
The order of lighting inside the home reflects the approach of Moshiach's days, when the public domain pushes into the Jewish home, as it does today through television, radio and the internet.
Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, the sign that a chiddush comes from kedushah is that another Jew builds a further chiddush on it; this is 'banim l'vanecha', grandchildren in Torah.
The Rambam places the laws of hallel in hilchos Chanukah, which shows that the root of hallel is Chanukah.
The Rav reads the Rambam's choice of words as a sign of something particular to Chanukah: the Rambam singles out this mitzvah alone as cherished.
He presents mosif v'holech, the nightly increase of the lights, as describing Chanukah itself: a time of adding in kedushah.
He speaks of engaging in holy matters not for oneself but for the sake of Hashem.
Milah expresses the eighth: nature makes a person with an orlah like the nations, and the Jew cuts it off and binds himself to Hashem above nature.
The oil miracle broke the bounds of arithmetic itself: the oil was no longer limited by how much a measure of oil can burn, so it burned exactly eight times as long.
Torah was given on the fiftieth day, the first day of the eighth week after seven times seven, so Torah too belongs to the eighth, and Chanukah is the Yom Tov of Torah's victory.
Zos Chanukah breaks the one-nasi-per-day pattern: one day reads several nesi'im, and on it all the leftover wicks of Chanukah burn together, a little day that holds a lot.

The Chozeh's reply shows that the Chanukah lights of even an informer revealed a light that shone in all worlds, more than his other mitzvos, because they uncover the hidden light of Moshiach in a Jew.

The dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan is not over the relative worth of Torah and tefillah, but over which a place enhances more: a shul's power to make tefillah accepted, or a beis medrash's power to magnify Torah.

Torah's inability to make miracles beyond nature comes from its greatness, not its weakness: nature is the Torah's own law, and a tzaddik who changes the order of Creation is in effect changing the Torah.

The Mikdash is where heaven ends and earth begins, so the heavenly order, beyond place, time and reckoning, applies there; miracles there are not a change of nature but nature of heaven dictated by the Torah.
The oil that held for eight days was the same kind of miracle as the few defeating the many, so the lights served as a mirror in which the hidden miracle of the war could be seen.
'Zeidim b'yad oskei sorasecha' in Al HaNissim names the source of the victory: the wicked fell into the hands of those who toil in Torah, because the miracle was made through Torah.
In Yosef's first dream he only watches from outside; in the second the whole holy structure, Yaakov and the Shechinah, must come down to him in his exile, so that he not sink there.

Placing the Chanukah light below ten tefachim, where the Shechinah never went, is a bikur cholim: in a festival of exile the great come down to the sick, as Hashem made Chizkiyahu ill so that Yeshayahu would come to him.

The blue of a flame, which consumes the wick, is Beis Shammai's midas hadin; the white, which gives light to others, is Beis Hillel's rachamim; and the 'borei' and 'me'orei' of their dispute follow from this.

Beis Shammai decrease the lights because they put sur mera first; Beis Hillel increase because aseh tov comes first and draws the sur mera after it, so a Jew should not wait to clean himself of sins before beginning.
The years of yeshiva are the 'chinuch' of a life: the oil poured in then must be enough to burn 'until the foot leaves the market', through the long years of parnassah outside the beis medrash.
The Torah is like the wife of whom it says 'beiso zo ishto': even when a Jew is away from the Gemara, his home and life must be run by it, so that his halichos become halachos.

The heavenly voice about Chanina ben Dosa still speaks in every generation, because each generation has a 'Chanina', one who knows that all he has is a free gift; the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh came from that same awareness.
The Gemara's answer to 'Mai Chanukah' is not an explanation but the eight days themselves: since Chanukah is above reason, the full answer cannot be given, and that is itself the answer.
The name Chashmonaim holds the letters of shemen and ches (eight), with the remaining letters spelling 'mai', the Gemara's question.

The only Chanukah law hinted in the Mishnah, placing the light below ten handbreadths, comes through Rebbi of the house of Dovid, because the aspect of Moshiach is to bring the highest light down to the lowest place.
The Ramban's reading, that Aharon's eternal share is Chanukah, and the Chiddushei HaRim's, that his menorah was hidden still burning, are one: both mean the hidden light of Chanukah.
Like the blessing of Shemini Atzeres, which does not leave when the day leaves because death was decreed only on this-worldly things, Chanukah's eighth day is never nullified.
Rashi's kal vachomer in the middle of the Yosef story teaches that the Torah's 'Hashem found the sin' about the pure shevatim exists so one can reason that He searches even more for merit.
The 'lo chen' of the wicked is their denial of the hidden, and for that reason they have no standing in the judgment completed on Zos Chanukah.
The Rav reads the Tzvi LaTzaddik's caution, that he would not have said an answer unknown to the Rishonim were it not the truth, as a sign that a new answer on Chanukah is itself a new revelation.

Because reality in this world follows the psak, as with the Rambam on the Mishnah in Niddah, each chacham's answer about the first night does not merely explain the past but brings a new kind of miracle into his own generation.
The answer of an empty flask with only a trace of oil was revealed specifically to our generation, because only such a miracle fits a generation that is itself an empty vessel.
The seal of the Kohen Gadol on the flask is the point of emunah inherited from Avraham Avinu, called a Kohen Gadol in the Midrash, which no Greek influence can defile even when the flask is empty.
The Rav reads 'dor ledor yeshabach' with the Beis Aharon: precisely because generations grow worse, their small avodah is more precious, so the world grows better.
The eighth light, which stood empty all of Chanukah, is a picture of the empty souls of the end of days, and its lighting on Zos Chanukah shows that they too are lit.

Beha'aloscha repeats that the menorah is mikshah down to its base because it speaks of the Chanukah menorah, teaching that the lowest souls are not attached pieces but one piece with the lights above.
The Rav reads the twelve days of the nesi'im as their Yom Tov and Chanukah as the Yom Tov of Aharon and his tribe, so that the Ramban's Chanukah lights are Aharon's own festival.
In Parshas Masei Aharon's age and his passing on Rosh Chodesh Av are given because there he stands for the Beis Hamikdash, the parshah of the journeys speaking of the exiles.
The menorah of the future Beis Hamikdash is being built in Heaven by the Chanukah lights of all generations, each adding its part.
The verse says 'beha'aloscha', raising the lights, and not kindling, because it speaks of the Chanukah menorah, where a new light is added each day.
'Mikshah hi ad yerechah ad pirchah' teaches that the lowest generations, who make the base, are one piece with the great ones who made the flowers.
The chasimah of Zos Chanukah is made by each Jew with his own hands, through his avodah with the Chanukah lights, Hallel and Al Hanisim.

The Rav reads 'ken asah es hamenorah' in Beha'aloscha as speaking of the Chanukah menorah: Aharon's lighting prepared the Chashmonaim's menorah and every Jew's menorah, which is why the only detail repeated there is mikshah.
The menorah's unlit lamps are not idle: they stand for the nations and the 'decreasing' side of the miracle, so lighting with empty lamps is as much a mitzvah and pirsumei nisa as the full ones.
The Rav explains the oil miracle as the 'long days' of Moshiach shining then: one day stretched to eight, like the long days that will follow the exile of Edom.
The seven dark lamps left on the first night correspond to the seven kings of Edom of whom the Torah says 'and he died'; of the eighth it does not say so.
The halachic requirement that a brachah not be made over empty vessels explains why the menorah must be one piece: joined to a lit lamp, the empty lamps are not an empty vessel.
Following the Sfas Emes that Chanukah continues Sukkos, Zos Chanukah is its Shemini Atzeres: the nations, who shared in the seven days, have no part, and all eight lamps are full and holy.

The Rav explains Aharon's eternal lighting through the Arizal's teaching on the soul of a tzaddik joining one who does his favorite mitzvah: Aharon, who never changed in his lighting, is drawn into every Jew who lights Chanukah candles, and this is why every Jew becomes a kohen on Chanukah.
Hoda'ah, the heart of Chanukah, is Aharon's middah of hod, and hod is the Bais HaMikdash; the Rav adds that hoda'ah equals 'Aharon HaKohen' in gematria.

The Rav explains why an informer was protected while lighting: the Chanukah light is the hidden light of Moshiach, and lighting kindles the hidden light in a person's own soul, so at that moment no harm could touch him.

On Zos Chanukah judgment is according to how a Jew will look in the days of Moshiach, by his hidden good; therefore even a small teshuvah, according to one's strength, is accepted then, which explains the Ruzhiner's saying that what tzaddikim achieve on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur a simple Jew can achieve on Zos Chanukah.

Following the Meiri, the Rav reads the precedence of shalom bayis as avoiding a quarrel between husband and wife over whose mitzvah to do, and explains that Chazal revealed the greatness of peace specifically through the Chanukah light because Chanukah is the Yom Tov of Aharon, lover of peace.

The Rav reads 'a man according to his praise' in Mishlei as: just as the crucible purifies silver and the furnace gold, praising Hashem purifies a person, and after such davening the light hidden in the Torah is revealed to him.
The Rav reads 'kol kesef hakelim' at the end of the Nesi'im as the moment the tribes stop being counted one by one and are counted as one, and this is what Zos Chanukah means.
The custom of burning the leftover wicks together on Zos Chanukah shows that the thirty-six masechtos, each with its own halachos, merge into one flame.
Burial of Avraham proves Yishmael's teshuvah not by learning, davening or fasting, but because he let his younger brother Yitzchak go first.
Only Chanukah and a few others are introduced with 'What is...?' because, like the Exodus, it comes from the fiftieth gate, and that level is awakened through questions.
'Mikshah te'aseh hamenorah' equals in gematria 'the third Beis HaMikdash'; the menorah alone was already part of the third Beis HaMikdash.
The empty cups on the one-piece menorah are not empty: they stand for Jews whose hidden light will shine when Moshiach comes, and Hashem judges by that.
The Rav reads 'pach shel shemen' as a jar that had held oil and was almost empty: all eight nights burned from its leftover drops, a light that belongs to the level of eight, beyond counting.
Rosh Hashanah, before letters existed, is served with the shofar's breath alone; Chanukah brings that same breath of life down into speech, as hallel and thanks.
The Gemara asks where the blessing over mitzvos comes from specifically in the laws of Chanukah because the first night's light matches Berachos, the first masechta.
The Torah totals the nesi'im's offerings on Zos Chanukah, though anyone could add them up, to show that on that day everything joins into one.

Applying Rav Chaim Vital's teaching that a soul who excelled in a mitzvah joins whoever does it, the Rav suggests that Aharon HaKohen joins every Jew who lights; this is how 'yours is greater than theirs' applies to all.
It works in both directions: since the hidden Menorah still burns, every Jew's Chanukah lighting also kindles Aharon's Menorah.
Precisely because Shemini Atzeres has no reason of its own, it shows Hashem's love: a distant relative needs a reason to attend a simcha, a father does not.
Chanukah is greater than Shemini Atzeres in closeness: there the Jews come up to Hashem, here Hashem comes down to the souls scattered in the street.
On Zos Chanukah Hashem does not ask the Jews to stay with Him above, as on Shemini Atzeres; He says that He will stay below with them.
Twelve nesiim of Israel stand against twelve princes of Yishmael and of Esav who lead the sitra achra, and the korbanos of the nesiim read on Zos Chanukah nullify them.
Yehuda's long retelling of what everyone already knew is read as an act of emunah: going over every detail so as to agree to and accept Hashem's guidance in each one.
The Rav applies the same idea to the end of Chanukah: one reviews what was said during the days only to settle them within oneself and pack them up to take along.
Bris milah on the eighth day is the Jew's answer to nature: nature says he was born with an orlah, and the Jew, coming from the eighth world, laughs at nature.

The final sealing of Zos Chanukah works by the Chanukah miracle's rule of 'the few in the hands of the many': a small point of mitzvos prevails over many sins, which is why it is for those who could not be acquitted on Rosh Hashanah.
The 'western wall' in a shul, where the plain Jews sit, is linked to the ner maaravi and to the Kosel Hamaaravi: what seems lowest holds the point that is never extinguished or destroyed.
The verse 'selach na' contains the initials of Chanukah only from 'hazeh' on, because on Chanukah sin is not mentioned at all.
Zos Chanukah relates to the whole of Chanukah as the mitzvah tantz relates to a wedding: the final moment that leaves its impression on the whole life that follows.
Although each nasi had his own day, on Zos Chanukah all of them are read and 'enter' that day, which makes it the gathering of all of Chanukah.
Calculation suits an individual's life, but the hanhagah of Klal Yisrael as a whole is above calculation, so its outcomes come as surprises no one can foresee.
Before Hashem a single Jew is a 'rov', a majority, unlike the world's view in which one Jew counts for nothing.
The Chashmonaim went to war for Hashem's sake, yet Hashem made the miracles not for Himself but for the Jews, to show His love for them.
Ordinary singing does not make a meal a seudas mitzvah, but at the Chanukah meal it does, because praise and thanksgiving are the very mitzvah for which Chanukah was established.

The division of roles, that a kohen may not be king and the king must come from Yehudah, belongs to this measured world; in the eighth world above measure one person can hold them all, which is why the first Chashmonaim were permitted both.
The Masorah counts words, not verses, only in Mikeitz, the Chanukah parsha, because a word joins letters, which stand above speech and comprehension.

The two orders of the tribes match the two views: for Beis Shammai the last is Binyamin, the last stone of the choshen and the place of the Beis Hamikdash; for Beis Hillel it is Dan, the gatherer who brings back what the others lost.
As the generations descend, they need more time for teshuvah, so a later sealing on Zos Chanukah was revealed only in later generations.
On the eighth day several nesi'im are included in one day, because above measure the little holds the much, like the small cruse of oil.
The lean cows' standing before swallowing the fat ones is read as the astonishment of the animal soul and the sitra achra before the hidden greatness of a Jewish soul.
Pharaoh's omission of the standing from his retelling reflects his shame at admitting that he himself is overawed by the strength of a Jew.
Pharaoh's words that the swallowed cows could not be recognized are called a lie: the hidden Jewish soul remains and is ultimately effective.
What a gentile cannot even recognize as a tzarah, a life without Torah and mitzvos, was for the Jews of the Chashmonaim a real tzarah, and that is why Hashem marveled and saved them.
The Rambam singles out Chanukah alone of the mitzvos as very dear because it came with mesiras nefesh, just as Avraham swore by the milah because it came to him through pain.
Giving one's own life is hard, but demanding mesiras nefesh of others is much harder, and the Rayatz demanded it of his chassidim.
The Rav reads the Midrash that Yaakov 'did not believe' as referring not to Yaakov himself, the root of bitachon, but to the faithless souls included in him.
The Me'or Einayim's lesson that disqualified oils are lit on Chanukah is applied to fallen souls: a Jew whom Shabbos cannot kindle, Chanukah can.
Yaakov is the trunk of the tree and Shabbos, the middle blessing, while the twelve tribes correspond to the twelve middle blessings of the weekday prayer.
Chanukah is the answer to Yaakov's plea: instead of the souls rising with Shabbos, the Shechinah comes down below ten to the place of darkness.
The Alter Rebbe's path is that of Shabbos, raising chassidim upward, while the later Chabad Rebbes took the path of Chanukah, going down to the lowest to bring them up to Shabbos.
Forgiving strangers who wronged him puts a man above Yosef, who forgave only his own brothers, to whom one is anyway bound to show mercy.
The total of a hundred and twenty is not twelve times ten but a new reckoning, in which the twelve tribes can no longer be told apart and only one Klal Yisroel remains.
The wagons, one for every two nesi'im, were the preparation for the mizbe'ach's inauguration: they broke down the partitions each tribe had around itself.
The verse's second 'this is the inauguration of the mizbe'ach, after it was anointed' points to a renewed inauguration still to come, which again depends on unity among Jews.
The brothers' silence toward Yosef, which Rashi credits to their honesty, finds its repair in Vayigash, where they speak with him without any gap between mouth and heart.
The blessing 'she'asa nissim' is not thanks for the oil alone; it acknowledges that the source of miracles is open now, so everything happening today comes through miracles.
Chanukah's eight days reach beyond the seven days of creation that set the order of nature; they draw down the separate order of miracles into time.
Just as during Sefirah everything a person feels and says relates to that day's sefirah, on Chanukah even the kugel, the gefilte fish and the wine hold miracles.
Chanukah is hod, the aspect of miracle, and therefore a time of hoda'ah, thanksgiving.
Even on the first night, when the oil was naturally enough, the light burned from the source of miracles, which is why a blessing on miracles is said that night too.

Barrenness is not only a woman without children: one whose davening does not go and who sees no fruit in his Torah is also 'barren', and Chanukah, a time of pekidas akaros, is when he can ask for help.
Zos Chanukah is the counterpart of Shemini Atzeres, so it carries the ushpiz of Shlomo HaMelech, and his avodah defines the day.

Chanukah begins at the end of the month, when the moon cannot be seen, and runs into Teves, the month of Esav: holiness breaks into the very time that belongs to the other side, just as the light goes into the reshus harabim.
Shlomo is the moon in its fullness, fifteen generations from Avraham like the fifteen days from the molad to the full moon; the Rav links the full moon to the daughters of kings through a gematria.

Shlomo's many wives were not what a simple reading suggests: as daughters of kings, heads of their nations, they were his way of bringing the seventy nations under holiness, and through them even the chief kelipos, the two harlots, submitted to him.
Purim and Chanukah are 'stations' between Sukkos and Pesach, given because after the churban the influence of the festivals could no longer carry a Jew through the year.

In the mashal of the queen, after two exiles Knesses Yisrael will not come back on her own; the king himself must lift her from the mud, and the light of Moshiach revealed each Chanukah is that lifting.
Although Shemoneh Esrei is said in the highest world, before the King, one asks there even for simple needs, because tefillah is said according to its plain meaning and there is no one else to ask.
Leaving before the end of davening is like a shopper who fills his cart, pays, and walks out without his bag: he loses the bounty he already earned.
The Imrei Emes's call to learn Chofetz Chaim broke the divide between chassidim and Litvaks, which fits the sefer's whole purpose: that there be no division among Jews.
Every time a person holds back a word he wants to say because the Chofetz Chaim forbids it, he is practicing yiras shamayim and conquering the yetzer, all day long.
The Chanukah lights of every generation accumulate; they are the chinuch of the light of Moshiach, just as a chanukas habayis precedes the full Beis HaMikdash.

The nations' cry that the Jews are robbers in Eretz Yisroel is exactly what Rashi addresses at the start of the Torah, and the Rav sees in it a sign that the light of Moshiach is breaking through, a reason for joy.
Zos Chanukah gives a simple Jew the power of prayer that a tzaddik has on Rosh Hashanah.
The words 'for Your salvation we hope all day', said three times daily, are themselves the answer to the question at the judgment whether one hoped for the redemption.
The Rav stresses that the Rambam requires not only believing in Moshiach but awaiting him, and that 'awaiting' is the Rambam's own word.
He identifies malchus Romi, the fourth kingdom, with the European nations and with America, whose people are immigrants from Europe.
Aharon's consolation was not only the lighting in his own day: his ner hama'aravi never went out, and the Chanukah lights of every generation draw from it.
'Zos Chanukah' refers to Aharon's own dedication, which had no day of its own among the princes and continues to this day.
Because the Chanukah miracle came from mesirus nefesh above nature, its mitzvah too asks for more than a person's means, and through that effort one comes to feel the light of the mitzvah.
The Yom Tov of Chanukah is placed inside the Hallel itself: it is the praise that makes the day a Yom Tov, which is why songs of praise turn the meal into a seudas mitzvah.
As Hashem sent Lot the angels so he would have the merit of hospitality, the new chance for kiruv is a mitzvah sent from Heaven to give Klal Yisrael merit before the ingathering of the exiles.

The ten utterances of creation were hidden, but at Yetzias Mitzrayim they were turned into the ten plagues that six hundred thousand Jews saw, so the Exodus is the visible proof that Hashem created the world; this is why the first commandment mentions the Exodus and not creation.

The plagues run backwards against the utterances: Bereishis, the first and most important utterance, is the beginning, and so the last plague, the firstborn, struck the beginning of Mitzrayim and was the most important plague.
Bereishis has no 'and He said' because it came before speech existed; it created the very power of speech, so only from the second utterance on can the Torah say 'and G-d said'.
Bread is three times the Name Havaya (78), the salt it is dipped in is again 78, and matzah equals three times the Name with its filled-in letters (135), so matzah is a higher bread.
Chametz is flour plus time plus place: time makes it rise and it takes up more space, while matzah, baked fast, is not ruled by time and place and so belongs above this world.

Hebrew is written from right to left because Yidden start from the right side, chesed, while Esav's nations write from left to right, din; Nisan's letters run forward through the alef-beis and Tishrei's run backwards.
The makkos ran in reverse order to the maamaros, starting from the earthly and working up to the heavenly, so that Hashem's control was shown at every level of creation.
The renewal of nature in spring is the filtering down of the heavenly renewal of Nissan, and a person who stays old while everything around him is renewed falls behind his own surroundings.
Animals each embody one trait and act predictably, while man contains all ten, which is why bread, a mixture, is the food of man.
Lechem equals three times twenty-six, the plain Shem Havayah, while matzah equals three times forty-five, the Shem Havayah spelled out in full, so matzah is a far higher food.

There are two beginnings of the year, Nissan with mercy and Tishrei with judgment, and one who places himself under Nissan's reishis through good matzos is already freed from the authority of Tishrei's judgment.
Every Nisan since Creation is not the original but an offshoot of the Rosh Chodesh Nisan on which Adam was created, the Nisan meant to bring the world into an everlasting Shabbos.
Just as a soul can return as a gilgul or enter another as an ibbur, a time can be 'reincarnated': the original Nisan was brought down again into the Nisan of Yetzias Mitzrayim and of the Mishkan.
An unexpectedly elevated Shabbos, felt after the mikveh, can be an ibbur: the soul of a tzaddik connected to a mitzvah one did has entered him for a while to help.
Kareis applies to only two positive mitzvos, milah and korban Pesach, because both belong to Avraham Avinu and both are the covenant binding a Jew to Hashem.

Lechem equals three times the Name Havaya (78), and matzah is that lechem with the Name spelled out in full (three times 45, the value of Adam), so eating matzah makes a person the 'Adam' of 'na'aseh adam'.
Since Nisan is the new year for kings, when Hashem appoints new heavenly ministers and kings, the time calls for Klal Yisrael to proclaim Hashem alone as King.
The Rav turns the war in Iraq into a scale for mitzvos: a blatt Gemara is a 'MOAB' bomb, a blatt Gemara with Tosafos is a missile that does not miss, and Amen yehei shmei rabba is a Patriot missile.
Since prophecy ended for individuals but not for Klal Yisrael as a whole, a minhag that all Jews take on is a prophecy from Hashem, fitted to the tikkunim that particular time needs.
The reading of the Nesi'im in Nissan is a weapon against Yishmael, whose twelve Nesi'im are subdued by the Nesi'im of Yisrael; without them Yishmael would have destroyed the Jews.

Through Reb Levi Yitzchak, the Rav shows that women scrubbing and kashering for Pesach are, without knowing it, destroying the yetzer hara, and every piece of chametz scrubbed off may be a whole enemy division.

Rashi's explanation that Og came while Avraham was baking matzos shows that the war against the four kings was on Pesach, linking the four kingdoms of galus to the four elements through which chametz is destroyed.
The worst chametz is atzvus; the Rav ties being an 'adam' on Rosh Chodesh Nissan, when Adam was created, to overcoming Yishmael, the 'pere adam'.

The Rav reads the history of Nisan as successive, ever more localized attempts at the perfect world of creation: the whole world with Adam, one nation at Yetzias Mitzrayim, one place in the Mishkan, until the fourth Nisan restores it on the large scale.

The seven days in which the Mishkan was built and taken apart mirror Hashem's own repeated attempts in Nisan, teaching that a disappointment in one's relationship with Hashem is a reason to get up and try again.

Chesed must be harnessed: the Jewish lunar calendar of chesed is aligned with the solar year of din, while the Arabs' purely lunar year lets their festival drift through the seasons, and the gentiles use the sun alone.

Matzah equals three times Mah (45) while bread equals three times Havaya (26), showing that matzah belongs to the world of Mah, a world one can only ask about; this is why the Seder opens with Mah Nishtanah.

Bread needs time to rise and so takes up space, while matzah is allowed no time and does not rise, so it stands above the two dimensions that define this world, the same 'when and where' on which witnesses are examined.
Kares for chametz is the opposite of the kesher, the bond with Hashem, that Pesach creates as the beginning of the year's festivals, which is why only one with a bris may eat the korban Pesach.
Rosh Chodesh Nissan recurs in history as a series of new beginnings: the creation of man, the Exodus and the setting up of the Mishkan, with a fourth still awaited.
Hashem's repeated 'attempts' at creation, like the Rosh Chodesh offering for diminishing the moon, are meant as a model for a Jew who fails and must begin again.
Na'aseh adam is renewed each Nissan: when all creation rejuvenates, a person who does not renew himself has excluded himself from creation.
Being an Adam does not mean erasing the animal traits of one's mazal, but ruling over them and raising them for avodas Hashem, like rising like a lion in the morning.
The kares for chametz, unlike the lesser punishments on Shavuos and Sukkos, shows that Pesach is the bond itself between Hashem and Klal Yisroel, so its opposite is being cut off.
The first failure, the sin of the Tree of Knowledge, is undone on Pesach: chametz is the Tree of Knowledge, and matzah, the food of emunah, is the Tree of Life that Hashem intended from the start.
Matzah equals three times the filled-out Name of Hashem (45), and geulah also equals 45, so matzah is three times geulah and carries the very Names with which Hashem redeemed the Jews from Mitzrayim.

Since it was the holy Names and not the flour and water that took the Jews out of Mitzrayim, the matzah eaten today is the identical matzah, worth more than an ancient piece an archaeologist might dig up.
Yaakov taking the blessings on the night of Pesach, when the treasuries of dew open, may be a hint to the custom of 'stealing' the afikoman at the Seder.
The Haggadah keeps multiplying the count of the plagues because saying them activates them: the more plagues counted, the more blows to the enemy and the more healing for the Jews.
Tashbisu equals the gematria of Shema Yisrael, and Vaizasa, the tenth son of Haman, equals Moshiach ben David, so destroying all ten parts of the chametz prepares the way for Moshiach.
Sukkos is the climax of the Yomim Tovim, yet Pesach, like an embryo, is the beginning, and the beginning is the main thing.
The kareis attached only to Pesach shows that Pesach is the bond with Hashem; its opposite, the kesher, is like a ring of kiddushin between a Jew and the Ribono shel Olam.
Matzah is not a mitzvah one does but one ingests, so its emunah becomes part of one's bones; for a Jew emunah is not information but part of him, in his genes.
Every animal eats food that matches its middah, a lion red meat for gevurah and a sheep white kernels for chesed, while man, who includes everything, eats bread, which includes all ten.
Lechem, 78, is three times Hashem's Name; matzah, 135, is three times its filled-out form of 45, so the bread is only a capsule while matzah holds the Name in its fullness.
Because the holy names of Yetzias Mitzrayim are in our matzah just as in theirs, one can say 'Ha lachma anya', this is the bread they ate, with a clear conscience.
The days of preparation before Pesach are themselves days of joy, like the kohanim's seven days of miluim before they began the avodah in the Mishkan.
Maariv was only a reshus not because it is lesser, but because, as the tefillah of Yaakov, it belongs to a higher world that not everyone is ready for.
Tikkun Chatzos is the tefillah of Dovid HaMelech, and Melaveh Malkah, the fourth seudah, corresponds to it as the seudah of Dovid.
Morning is called tzafra after the birds and night ramsha after the creeping creatures that sing then, while a Jew sings both by day and by night.
Matzah equals three times 45, the filled-out Name of Hashem that equals adam, so it holds a deeper holiness than ordinary bread, which is three times 26.
'Ha lachma anya' is literally true: the geulah inside the matzah is identical to what our forefathers ate, and only the outer envelope of flour and water is different.

The four ways of destroying chametz mirror the four elements that come from the four letters of Hashem's Name: scattering to the wind, throwing into the sea, burning, and bitul, which makes it like the dust of the earth.
Avraham Avinu's dust that became weapons against the four kings was itself bitul chametz, nullifying the four kingdoms, and he did it on Pesach.

The authority of the nations is captured malchus of the Jewish people, passed from Bavel to Madai, Yavan and Rome, and it must be returned to Mashiach; Yishmael is not counted because his rule is his own.
The same four klipos appear as the four layers at a bris, the four marks of tzara'as and the four years of orlah; the fourth, Edom, is raised rather than cut off, since it holds kedushah.
Chametz, fit to eat, is Edom, from whom converts came, while se'or, unfit to eat, is Yishmael, from whom no good came.
Each of the four cups has two sides: the wine spilled at the makkos is a cup of poison for Mitzrayim, and the refilled cups are the Jews' cups of geulah.
Pinchas, who is Eliyahu, avenged the sale of Yosef only on Midian; the main sellers, the Yishmaelim, remain for him, which links the cup of Eliyahu to the reckoning with Yishmael.
The Rav reads kares and kashrus as opposites: just as eating chametz on Pesach cuts the bond with Hashem, eating matzah ties it, a level of connection no other Yom Tov's mitzvah reaches.

The spring that reawakens nature in Nisan is the earthly reflection of the joy in Heaven over the new bond with Klal Yisrael, the song of the Chassan and Kallah that Shlomo HaMelech put into Shir Hashirim.

Bread equals three times the Name of Hashem (78), while matzah equals three times its full spelling, 'Mah' (135): matzah draws from a holiness so high it can only be asked about, which is why the Seder begins with questions.
The matzah is the key of birth that Hashem keeps for Himself, and the Targum calls matzah 'patira', an opening, like 'peter rechem'.

Following the Ba'al HaTanya, the matzah's flour and water are only a capsule; inside is the same light of Yetzias Mitzrayim that the Jews ate in Mitzrayim, so the matzah is the original and not a copy.
The tal of 'my head is filled with dew' is the first three letters of the Name in full spelling (39), which descends to the final hei, Klal Yisrael, and that is the matzah.

The Rav reads the halachic status of a pilegesh spiritually: unlike a wife, who merges with her husband, a pilegesh keeps her own identity, so Timna's holy longing passed through Amalek's line without ever becoming part of it.
Esther's seudah destroyed Haman by drawing him out of tumah to the edge of kedusha, which he could not enter, so that he was left with no source of life at all.
Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, a descendant of Haman, is the one who taught that when Adar enters one increases simcha, because his root lay in the simcha Haman drew from Esther's Pesach seudah.

The Rav connects the Haggadah's Bnei Brak to Haman's descendants: the talmidim who could not reach Krias Shema of Shacharis carried Zeresh's attempt to stop Mordechai's morning Shema, and the Tannaim chose Pesach to free them.
The Rambam's pairing of Shema Yisrael with 'va'achos Lotan Timna' becomes the story of Bnei Brak: the Tannaim lifted the children of the passuk Menashe mocked to the level of Shema.
Morning is called tzafra because the birds (tziporim) sing then, and night ramsha because the crawling creatures sing then; a Jew is not limited to either, but sings to Hashem morning and night.
Pesach is lower than Shavuos and Sukkos in Hallel, yet only Pesach carries kares: kares means being cut off from Hashem, and Pesach, being the bond itself, is where that cutting-off applies.
Just as the first blessing of Shemoneh Esrei ends with Magen Avraham alone and not all three Avos, so among the Regalim Pesach is the 'point' from which everything begins.
The only two positive mitzvos whose neglect carries kares, milah and the korban Pesach, are both bound up with Avraham Avinu, whose Yom Tov is Pesach.
Taking out the Pesach dishes after twelve months is like seeing a friend after twelve months, a kind of techiyas hamesim.

Just as an esrog is a plain citrus fruit all year and becomes a holy object on Sukkos, the Pesach matzah is an envelope for holy Names of emunah and geulah, the same Names that took the Jews out of Egypt.
Lechem equals three times the Name Havayah, while matzah equals three times that Name spelled out in full (45), showing that matzah holds higher holy Names than ordinary bread.

The ten plagues, counted from the last, mirror the ten utterances of creation from the first: makkas bechoros against 'Bereishis', darkness against 'let there be light', locusts that hid the sky against the utterance of the firmament.
Because the whole of Nisan is yetzias Mitzrayim, the Haggadah's thought of starting the telling from Rosh Chodesh has a grain of truth.
Saying the plagues at the Seder breaks the klipah of heresy, brings downfall on the enemies of Israel, and draws emunah into the Jew.
The three dips of bread in salt allude to the Name Havayah three times, whose total of 78 is the gematria of lechem; with that strength a Jew learns, davens and fights the yetzer hara.
'Ha lachma anya' is literally true: the matzah is only an envelope, and the holy Names inside it are the very ones our forefathers ate in Egypt.
Just as no one would put on tefillin written carelessly, the matzah that serves as a Jew's os on chol hamoed should be baked with kedushah.

The Jewish custom of buying new clothes and painting the house for Pesach, rather than during Sefirah, is part of the renewal of all creation in Nissan, and a Jew must join that renewal inwardly as well.
A promised blessing that does not arrive is like money put into a pocket with a hole: the blessing comes but falls out, because the soul lacks a whole vessel to hold it.
Matzah works like a vitamin: just as each vitamin gives the body a particular strength, matzah gives the soul emunah, the level of Avraham Avinu.
Even a child's prayer for something trivial, or a prayer that one's team should win, is real emunah, since the one praying turns to Hashem knowing He can grant it.
The Lubliner revealed his notebook not to display his powers, which his talmidim knew anyway, but to teach that each of the first days of Nissan governs a whole month.
Like hand matzos and machine matzos, there are hand-made tefillos and machine tefillos; a quick davening on an assembly line is the latter.
The Torah opens with Bereishis rather than the mitzvah of the new moon because Bereishis alludes to the sun and to nature, and the world of nature was itself created for Yisroel.
Birchas HaChamah declares that the sun, the source of giving in nature, truly belongs to Yisroel, even while in exile Yisroel receives only the leftovers from the nations.
Rashi's reading of 'me'oros' as a curse means that luminaries serving to give light is itself a lack; their true role is for seasons, days and years, while the light should come from Hashem Himself.
Because a mitzvah done with a thing puts strength into it, Jews blessing the sun on the day that stands for Tammuz infuses the sun with Yisroel's power and is a sign that Esav's dominion will end.
The twenty-eight-year return of the sun to its starting point is also a call for a person to return to his own starting point, the upright state in which Hashem created him.
The Rav reads the letters of the months: the season of Nissan, 'aviv', runs alef-beis in order, the way of chesed, while Tishrei runs the alphabet backwards (tav-shin-reish), the way of din.

'Shanah' means repetition, and is related to 'yashan', old, and 'sheinah', sleep; so the nations, who have only a year, live in dormant repetition, while the Jewish 'chodesh' is the opposite, a waking renewal.

The light of the first day lacks 'vayehi ken' because 'ken' means something that stays in place, and that light was hidden on account of the wicked; this is the meaning of 'lo ken haresha'im', and that same hidden light will one day judge them.

'Yeshuos b'mekupos' means salvation on credit: just as the redemption from Egypt was paid for by the future acceptance of the Torah, a Jew may ask Hashem in Nissan for salvation now against the good he will do later.
Kiddush hachodesh shows the Jews stand above time: they decide when the month begins, even when mistaken, rather than time dictating their duties.
The Egyptians plowing over the hidden Jewish children is a symbol of the whole exile, and when the Jews are redeemed the Torah too will be redeemed, revealing new midrashim not yet disclosed.
The Rav describes chametz as made of three ingredients, flour, water and time; matzah lacks the third, and so it suits the exodus, which happened above time.
The first of anything is not yet time, since time is only the distance from a starting point; that is why the exodus had to be in the month called 'first'.
Witnesses are tested on time and place, and chametz, which time swells to fill more place than its truth, is a false witness, while matzah is a true one.
Roasting concentrates a thing and draws it into itself while cooking breaks it apart, so the korban Pesach is roasted to express oneness.
The frog alone in Perek Shirah says 'Baruch Shem', not a passuk, and quietly, because its song rises from places of tumah where words of Tanach may not be said.
R' Elazar ben Azaryah's retort 'go to Negaim and Oholos' points to their opening word 'two': a mixture of kedushah and tumah like the frog cannot be called 'one'.

From Sefer HaKanah the Rav shows that the letters of 'Baruch Shem kevod malchuso' are the only ones that can join with Hashem's name, and from this he draws the advice to bind oneself to those who are better.
Nissan is the 'pesichas ha'aron' of the calendar: as the opening of the aron is an eis ratzon, so in Nissan a Jew's prayer is more readily accepted than at any other time.
The small aleph of Vayikra can only be seen from close up; one far from Hashem reads 'vayikar' and sees coincidence, while one who draws near in Nissan sees that every event is a call from Hashem.
The custom of 'stealing' the afikoman may come from Yaakov, who on Pesach night took Yitzchak's blessing of tal in a way that looked like theft, while the Shechinah smiled on it.
Nissan is called 'Aviv' because it begins with aleph-beis in order, chesed, while Tishrei follows the reversed order, tav-shin-reish, the order of din.
The matzah's physical form is only a capsule for its spirituality, which is eternal; therefore 'ha lachma anya' is literally true, since the inner matzah is the one eaten in Egypt.
'Simcha' is linked to 'somech', leaning, since shin and samech interchange, and 'atzvus' to 'azuv', forsaken: joy is having Someone to lean on.
Leaning on the afikoman hidden under the pillow, though one may not lean on a sefer, shows that a Jew leans on Hashem Himself, since the matzah is His holy Names.
Each failed Nissan creation was followed by a smaller, more concentrated one: from the whole world, to Klal Yisrael, to a corner of holiness in the Mishkan where the intended ideal world would exist.
Hashem Himself 'did not tire' of renewing the world after failures, so a Jew who falls is taught to begin anew rather than despair.
The Targum's word for matzah, 'petira', means opening, linking matzah to opening the door at the seder, the opened heavens and the call 'open to Me' in Shir haShirim.
Chametz is dough that time has ruled over, eighteen minutes being the measure of time, and so it swells and takes up space; matzah is free of both time and place, like emunah.
Lechem equals three times the name Havayah, one for each of nefesh, ruach and neshamah, while matzah equals three times the name spelled out in full (45), a higher holiness.
The many times the word 'mah' appears in the Haggadah express emunah: one can only ask 'what', never fully know.
Hashem does not want a separate 'Pesach house' that chametz never touched; He wants the chametz removed and matzah brought into the very same place, as with the yetzer hara.

Rabbi Eliezer, a disciple of Beis Shammai whose way is din, holds the world was created in Tishrei, the time of din; Rabbi Yehoshua of Beis Hillel, whose way is chesed, holds it was created in Nissan, the month of chesed. Each follows his own approach.
The month is called 'aviv' because its letters, alef and beis, run forward in order, which is chesed, while the letters of Tishrei run backwards from the end of the alef-beis, which is din.
Trees shedding the 'white shrouds' of winter and putting on green in Nissan are a picture of techiyas hameisim, and Pesach is the time of techiyas hameisim.

Bread (lechem) equals three times the simple Name of Hashem, 78, but matzah equals three times the Name spelled in full, 45, which is 'adam'; so 'not by bread alone does adam live', and matzah makes a person into an adam.
On Chol HaMoed one does not wear tefillin because the matzah stands in their place; therefore matzah deserves the same standard one expects of tefillin.

From the builders of the Tower, who kept repeating 'havah' to put more impurity into it, the Bnei Yissaschar learns that in holiness too each repetition of 'l'shem matzas mitzvah' puts new holiness into the matzah.
Because every mitzvah is a remembrance of the Exodus, Pesach is not only the first festival but the embryo that contains all the festivals within it.

Like a ball, the round world has no natural top or center; only its Maker knows the point He began from, and that point, the foundation stone, is what makes the Beis Hamikdash 'higher than all places'.
The 'place causes' rule for the rebellious elder reflects that the Sanhedrin, the central souls from whom Torah goes out, has its full power only when seated at the world's root point.
The two opinions on when the world was created yield two centers of the Torah: Bereishis for Tishrei and the Kohen Gadol, and 'darosh darash Moshe', the middle word, for Nissan and Moshe the king.
The moon's waning is the earth's physicality coming between the sun and Knesses Yisrael, and the Rosh Chodesh atonement 'for Hashem' answers the questions this concealment raises against Him.

The Rosh Chodesh Nissan goat in the middle of the Torah was burned because that day revealed a taste of the end of days, when it will be clear Hashem never needed atonement, a reward for Aharon's silent faith.
The nations count by the solar 'shanah', meaning repetition, while Jews have the 'chodesh', renewal, the root of teshuvah.

By the at-bash sign, the sixth day of Pesach falls on the weekday of the Purim before it; the Rav reads this as Nissan revealing what was hidden in Adar, just as Vayikra's small aleph shows that the call was always one of love.
Since the Targum renders matzah with a word meaning opening, the Rav calls matzah the key that opens a Jew's heart to Hashem on Pesach, the festival of opening.

The world was created in Tishrei in deed but in Nissan in thought, because the Exodus, when Klal Yisrael became a nation, completed creation; this is why the first commandment speaks of the Exodus rather than of creation.

Chametz has stringencies no other prohibition has because it is the yetzer hara; Amalek, whose numerical value equals safek (doubt), is fought on Erev Pesach, and so the Beis HaMikdash, which follows the war on Amalek, is linked to Pesach.
Emunah is spiritual and does not cling to the body, so Hashem gave it in a capsule: matzah is ordinary flour and water that carries emunah inside it.
Simcha is tied to leaning (samach): joy is the feeling of having someone to lean on, while atzvus is the feeling of being abandoned, which is why idols, which cannot be leaned on, are called atzabim.
Haggadah comes from gid, a vein that carries life to the limbs, and from gad, mazal that flows down from its root: the Haggadah channels emunah and salvation from above.

Because matzah is the 'food of emunah' and emunah is the root of all the mitzvos, 'ushmartem es hamatzos' read as 'mitzvos' is not a mere wordplay: matzah truly holds all the mitzvos, and as one treats matzah so he will have mitzvos all year.
The visible matzah is like a capsule from the pharmacy: what one sees is only flour and water, the outer shell, while the real content inside is emunah.

Nissan's spring, when farmers water their fields and everything sprouts, is the time for a Jew to 'water' his emunah, and matzah and the four cups bring down halachah and yiras Shamayim for the whole year.

Just as speech aloud for avodah zarah draws a spirit of impurity into a house, speech aloud 'l'shem mitzvah' draws kedushah into the matzah, and repeating it many times adds more, as the generation of the dispersion repeated 'havah'.
The matzah absorbs the words spoken while baking it: just as it absorbs the telling of yetzias Mitzrayim, it can sadly absorb leitzanus.
With the Radbaz, the Rav says that with chametz the hint is itself the plain meaning: for other mitzvos the yetzer hara is a remez, but for chametz it is the very reason for its severity.

Following the Chiddushei HaRim, the Rav reads kares not only as a punishment but as a sign: a mitzvah whose neglect cuts a person off is one whose fulfillment binds him, so Pesach and milah are the mitzvos of attachment to Avraham and to Klal Yisrael.
The Rav contrasts the names of the months: the Torah's name for Nissan, Aviv, runs aleph-beis in order from the right, the way of chesed, while Tishrei runs the letters backward, the way of din.

Unlike a commemoration, each festival repeats its original event; so the spring awakening of nature is the renewal in heaven reaching down, and the person who sees the trees come back to life must ask why he should stay behind.

The ten plagues mirrored the ten utterances of creation in reverse: the first utterance created the 'first', and the last plague struck the firstborn; the second utterance was light, and the second-to-last plague was darkness.
'Would have' does not belong in a Jew's vocabulary: complaining about what would have happened had someone acted differently is a lack of faith in hashgacha pratis.

Chametz is made of flour, water and time, and once leavened it rises and takes up space, so it is ruled by time and place; matzah is kept from time and does not expand, and so it is the food of emunah, which is above time and place.
Bread is three times the Name Havayah in simple letters (3 × 26 = 78), while matzah is three times the Name spelled out in full (3 × 45 = 135), showing matzah's higher holiness.

The Rav reads the 'im' of the omer and of yovel as expressing not doubt about the obligation but that their level is above this world and cannot be grasped with certainty, like the Mikdash that must be sought.
Place, time and soul each have a 'king' that is their 'pele': the Mikdash, Nissan, and the king of Israel; and only the 'pele' of the soul, David, could find the 'pele' of place.

Just as Shmuel, head of the prophets, had to search out which son of Yishai was king, David had to toil to find the Mikdash; the Rav ties 'lishichno tidreshu' and 'som tasim alecha melech' together by gematria.
A father's hidden inner self appears in his son: David is Shabbos, the seventh, but his inner depth, yovel, was revealed in Shlomo, which is why David longed to build the Mikdash and Shlomo built it.

The fiftieth mention of the Exodus in the Torah, counting only mentions in praise, is in 'Arami oved avi', which is why it is expounded on the Seder night: it draws down the fiftieth gate and the coming of Moshiach.

Heaven made Hillel forget the law of the knife so that it would be revealed that his knowing that Pesach overrides Shabbos came from his soul's root as Shlomo, not only from his teachers, as he humbly claimed.

Haman and Yishmael are 'adam velo melech': even impure kingship holds a spark of accepting Hashem's kingship, as the Girgashi and Achashverosh show, but Yishmael has no king at all, only princes, and so his galus is the hardest.
Pesach belongs to Avraham because both are firsts: the first Jew and the first Yom Tov of the year, which opens with 'this month shall be for you the first of months'.
By eating matzah, the food of emunah, a Jew in a sense takes in Avraham himself: eating matzah is eating emunah.
Pesach was the turning point of Avraham's life, and the events of Sarah in Pharaoh's house, with plagues and gifts, foreshadowed the Exodus of his children.
The 'great wealth' promised to Avraham is read as emunah, worth more than millions and billions of dollars.
Moshiach will name the children one by one as the ones who brought him, because they learned, davened and guarded themselves from sin.

The three regalim are the inheritance of the three Avos: Pesach is Avraham's chesed and emunah, Shavuos, when the Torah was heard 'from the mouth of the Gevurah', is Yitzchak's, and Sukkos is Yaakov's; each is higher than the one before, yet Pesach remains the foundation.

Hashem wanted the clarity of emunah revealed at makkas bechoros to stay with the Jews, so He invested it in the matzah, a food, so that it would become part of their flesh, blood and bones; likewise every yom tov's gift is carried in its food.

Kareis means being cut off, so its opposite is being bound; that kareis applies to chametz, to the korban Pesach and to milah, which belongs to Avraham, shows that Pesach binds a Jew to Hashem more than Shavuos and Sukkos.
A great tzaddik and a simple Jew put on tefillin in exactly the same way; what makes the tzaddik's act greater is only the clarity of his emunah, and by this a Jew is measured.

The order of the makkos climbs through creation: blood in the water, the lowest element, then frogs, lice in the earth, wild animals on it, boils of fire, hail in the air, darkness in the luminaries, and the firstborn's souls above the heavens, answering Pharaoh that Hashem rules from bottom to top.
The ten makkos reveal the ten utterances of creation in reverse: makkas bechoros corresponds to 'Bereishis', darkness to 'let there be light', and the locusts to the firmament.

Telling a miracle can make it happen again, so saying the makkos at the Seder draws blows upon the enemies of Israel and healing upon the Jews, and the Haggadah's multiplication of makkos multiplies both.
Mitzrayim is 'meitzar yam': 'yam' equals fifty in gematria, and Egypt is what blocked the Jews from the fifty gates of understanding.

The rasha who denies yetzias Mitzrayim stands in the fiftieth gate, which is heresy; yet the Haggadah's 'one the Torah speaks of' means that even he can be pulled out through the telling of the Exodus.
Following his rebbe, 'lesaper' also means 'to count': the mitzvah includes counting the fifty mentions of yetzias Mitzrayim in the Torah that are in praise of Hashem's taking us out.
The severity of kares for chametz shows the reverse: as kares cuts a person off, Pesach binds him to Hashem.
The sefer Torah is holier than the sofer who wrote it because he was only a messenger, like a mailman who brings a letter he did not write; once the work is done his agency ends.
The physical matzah is only an envelope for the holy names within it, which are the same as those in the matzah eaten in Egypt; this is why one may say 'ha lachma anya', this is the bread.
The stringencies of Pesach follow from its being a beginning: what is laid at the start must be entirely firm.
Everything spiritual is reflected in the physical: the blossoming of trees in Nissan mirrors the spiritual beginning of the nation.
Pesach, where full Hallel is said only on the first day, and a bachur are both not yet at completeness.
The unearned light a bachur feels in learning and davening is like a chassan's gifts: a sign of the start of a bond, so important that a teshuvah treats their absence as grounds to break a shidduch.
Nissan should feel to a bachur like his own friend, since both are the days of growth.

The lowness of the last generations is itself their greatness: because they have fallen so low, they reach sparks from a root so high that the Tannaim and Amoraim could not reach them, and the redemption to come will be from the fiftieth gate, beyond the forty-nine of Egypt.
The kares for chametz and for missing the korban Pesach, absent on Shavuos and Sukkos, shows that Pesach binds a Jew to the very root, to emunah, even though the later festivals are greater.
The blessing Magen David is said only after maftir, the eighth aliyah, which corresponds to Moshiach and is above the world, because the world cannot yet make that blessing in its own place.
Yetzias Mitzrayim is the visible testimony of creation: the ten plagues reveal, in reverse order, the ten sayings by which the world was made, so both reasons for Shabbos say one thing.
A Jew who calls himself a kofer is only 'coated over', as the Torah uses the word for the pitch on the teivah; at a moment of danger he cries out to Hashem.
Matzah takes the place of tefillin as the sign of Pesach, so a matzah baked carelessly is like tefillin written by someone unfit.

Because a pilegesh has no true bond, Timna's line ran through Amalek like an insulated wire: the spark of her desire for Avraham's family passed through the generations without mixing in, which is why Haman's descendants could convert.

Esther invited Haman to her feast so that, by enjoying it, the holy spark in him would be freed; 'yavo hamelech veHaman hayom' holds Hashem's Name and equals in gematria 'they learned Torah in Bnei Brak'.
Following the Ruzhiner, Shaul's 'I have fulfilled the word of Hashem' meant that by sparing Agag he had brought Purim into the world, which is why Shmuel never rebuked him for it.
The difficulty of the people of Bnei Brak with the morning Krias Shema was inherited from Zeresh, who wanted to hang Mordechai in the morning before his Krias Shema.

Following the Ba'al Shem Tov's rule that one not obligated cannot exempt others, the Tannaim had to share the flaw of Haman's descendants; by missing the matzah, as the Jews did in Haman's time, they could repair them.
The fast that cancelled Pesach in Esther's time was the appeasement given to the Sitra Achra so that the great success of Purim could be established.
A Birkas Hachama on erev Pesach is greater than usual, because the war against Amalek, Shaul's against Agag and Moshiach ben Yosef's, falls on erev Pesach.
